catalog_citation: Abdul-Moomin, Abdul-Aziz. 2015. Aspects of Waali phonology. MPhil thesis, Department of Linguistics, University of Ghana, Legon. xviii+212 pp. (open full text via the Internet Archive capture 2026-09-06 of the ResearchGate PDF, DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.18741.23523)
catalog_locator: ch. 5 'Tonology': sec. 5.5-5.6, p. 136; sec. 5.7 'The Lexical Tone in Waali', p. 141; sec. 5.11 'Conclusion', p. 156
catalog_quote: But there are cases where some languages combine relative pitch and contour tones, such as Waali. In Waali verbs and nouns can be distinguished by contour tones. ... For the majority of tones however Waali can be described as a two-tone system language. 5.6 The Waali Tone and Tonal Patterm Waali is a tone language. Tones are the pitch variations that affect the lexical menaing of a word. ... Waali has two level tones H and L but in isolations it has four contrasting tone melodies underlyingly thus; High to Low falling (F), Low to High rising (R), Low and High. [p.141] Waali is a two-tone system language (high and low) but uses four tone melodies – high, low, rising and falling to distinguish meaning. Thus, these four tonal melodies in Waali are lexical tones. [p.156] This chapter discussed the tonal system of Waali. It was observed that Waali is a two-level tone (high-low) language (high, low) that exhibit four melodies in distinguishing the lexical word. This tonal system is similar to Dagbani and Gurune but interestingly different from those of its closest neighbours – Dagara, Dagaare and Birfʊɔr, which all have three-level tone system.

Waali is a tone language. Tones are the pitch variations that affect the lexical menaing of a word.. (Adonae, 2005). new_statements.rule_in_words: Waali is described as a lexical/grammatical tone language with two level tones (H, L; HL and LH contours on monosyllables in isolation), tone spreading and downstep/terracing. The thesis, the only full phonological description of Waali located, never mentions word stress or accent anywhere (the strings 'stress'/'accent' do not occur in its 230 pages); no statement on the position of any word-level prominence exists in the accessible literature.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: nouns vs verbs can be distinguished by contour tones (e.g. ʤu 'head' vs ʤu 'steal'); grammatical tone sections (5.9-5.10) are listed in the TOC but flagged 'Error! Bookmark not defined' and only partly present.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone on citation forms elicited with the SIL Comparative African Word List (SILCAWL) from Wa-town speakers, plus utterance-level downstep; no word-stress domain is defined because stress is not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis describes Waali as spoken in Wa town and surrounding villages (Upper West Region, Ghana) = Glottolog wali1263 / ISO wlx; the author (and Bodomo 1997, Dakubu 2005) treat Waali/Waale as a dialect within the Dagaare continuum, but the data and statements are specifically Waali, not Central Dagaare (daga1274) or Dagara/Birfor.

sources.locator: ch.5 'Tonology', sec. 5.5-5.6, p.136 (p.154); conclusion sec. 5.11, p.156 (p.174)
sources.note: Whole thesis is a phonology (inventory, syllable V/CV/CVC, harmony, processes, ch.5 'Tonology' pp.130-157). The word 'stress' / 'accent' occurs nowhere in the 230 pages. Ch.5 states Waali is a tone language with two level tones H and L, four surface melodies on monosyllables in isolation (H, L, HL falling, LH rising), lexical and grammatical tone, spreading, downstep/terracing; concludes it is a two-level tone language like Dagbani and Gurune (unlike three-level Dagara/Dagaare/Birfor).

tone.quote: There are also tonal contrasts in the language, and where my sources gave tone-marks I have preserved them (even laboriously blending the tone marks from the older version with the vowels from the newer in the phonemic transcription) without any way of knowing what is the system or the reliability or necessity of the markings. Vowel length is also clearly significant, indicating by the doubling of the letter for the long vowel
tone.locator: p. vii (end of 'Spellings' section, before 'Entry Structure')
tone.summary: Says the language has tonal contrasts and keeps tone marks (acute/grave) from earlier sources on some 600 transcriptions, but states no tone system and disclaims knowing it; vowel length contrastive.
